newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss name head of Nazi Victims task force.
newsitem.headline: Swiss name head of Nazi Victims task force.

text.p: Swiss Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti on Friday named an official from his ministry to head a task force to coordinate various inquiries into what happened to the wealth of Holocaust victims deposited in Swiss banks.
Thomas Borer, 39, an international lawyer and deputy secretary-general in the foreign ministry, will head the newly created Assets of Nazi Victims task force, the ministry said in a statement.

Borer was named just two days after Cotti announced he would form two new expert panels to probe mounting accusations that the unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims from Eastern Europe was used to compensate Swiss citizens for nationalised property.

Borer began his diplomatic career in 1987 and served as deputy head of the division for international law from 1989 to 1993. In 1993 he transferred to the Swiss embassy in Washington, where he was counselor for legal and political affairs. He returned to Berne in 1994.
Another foreign ministry task force, whose leader has yet to be named, will study compensation agreements Switzerland struck with then-communist governments in eastern Europe.

"The Task Force Assets of Nazi Victims is to ensure swift and coordinated action on the part of the Federal Authorities in all questions related to the complex issue of assets which arrived in Switzerland due to the Nazi Regime," the ministry said.

Borer's task force will assure close cooperation with the Swiss Federal Archives, the finance ministry, the justice and police ministry, Swiss diplomatic representations abroad, the Swiss National Bank and the Swiss Bankers Association.
It will also establish contact with both domestic and foreign groups and organisations interested in this question.
Switzerland has struggled to deal with sharp criticism from Jewish groups and influential U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato about the way it handled dormant accounts from Holocaust victims.

Critics got fresh ammunition from a study showing the Swiss paid Poland around 480,000 Swiss francs (now $382,800) and earmarked 325,000 francs for Hungary under secret deals that Jewish groups say robbed Holocaust victims of their wealth.

Worried about Switzerland's reputation abroad, the head of parliament's foreign affairs committee this week urged the government to be more decisive and do more than just react to a steady stream of damaging documents emerging from U.S. archives.
Switzerland is tracking down dormant accounts in three ways in addition to the creation of the two task forces.

A banking ombudsman is coordinating nearly 1,000 claims that have been submitted and an independent panel set up by Jewish groups and Swiss bankers will also comb banks' records for unclaimed wealth that may have escaped two previous sweeps.
Parliament is also set to give final approval in December to a panel of historians and experts empowered to lift strict banking secrecy and conduct a sweeping review of the era.
